opus-5.5.text:
I think simulation is absolutely essential, and frankly it's becoming one of the most important parts of the whole development and validation pipeline. If you think about the problem, the events that really matter for safety are rare. You can drive millions of miles and only encounter a handful of the truly challenging situations — someone running a red light at speed, a pedestrian emerging from behind a parked truck, unusual interactions at a construction zone. You simply can't rely on real-world driving alone to see enough of those cases, and you certainly can't repeatedly stage them on public roads to check whether a new version of your software handles them better.

So simulation lets us do a few things. First, it lets us replay and re-run the scenarios we have encountered, but with the new version of the stack in the loop, so we can see whether behavior improved or regressed. Second, it lets us create variations — perturb the timing, the speeds, the positions, the behaviors of other agents — and explore the space around a real event rather than just the single instance we logged. And third, it lets us synthesize scenarios that are very hard or dangerous to collect at all.

The key challenge, and where a lot of the research energy goes, is realism. A simulator is only as useful as it is faithful to the real world in the aspects that matter. There are really two parts to that. One is sensor realism — can you generate camera, lidar and radar data that your perception system responds to the same way it would in reality? The other, which I think is equally important and sometimes underappreciated, is behavioral realism. When you change what your car does, the other agents in the scene need to react plausibly. If you just replay logged trajectories, the other drivers become non-reactive ghosts, and you get either unrealistic collisions or unrealistically easy situations. So building good learned models of how humans drive, walk and cycle, models that are reactive, diverse and realistic, is a central piece of making simulation trustworthy.

And there's a nice synergy there: the same kinds of models we build for behavior prediction and planning on the car are closely related to the agent models we need in simulation. Advances in one feed into the other.

Ultimately, I see simulation as how you scale evaluation. Real-world driving remains the ground truth and gives you the data and the long tail, but simulation is where you get statistical confidence — running enormous numbers of scenarios, measuring safety-relevant metrics, and making the case that the system is ready. Neither replaces the other; you need them working together.

r001.rationale: The response says simulation is needed to test rare safety situations and describes testing the vehicle against scenarios involving other road users, including pedestrians and drivers.

r002.rationale: It identifies learned models of human driving, walking, and cycling as a central part of trustworthy simulation, communicating the use of machine learning models to build simulator behavior for vehicle evaluation.

fable-5.1.text:
Simulation is absolutely central for us. If you think about it, the self-driving problem is really a problem of the long tail. The common cases, driving down a road, stopping at a light, we handled those a long time ago. What makes the problem hard is the rare and unusual situations: a pedestrian stepping out from behind a parked truck, a cyclist running a red light, debris falling off a vehicle in front of you. You can't rely on encountering those events often enough in the real world to test against them, and you certainly don't want to be creating dangerous situations on public roads to see how the vehicle responds.

So simulation gives us a few things. First, it gives us scale. We drive orders of magnitude more miles in simulation than we do on real roads, and we can do it every day for every version of the software. Second, it gives us control. We can take a scenario we saw once in the real world and vary it: make the pedestrian a little faster, put them a meter closer, change the weather, change the time of day. One real event becomes thousands of test cases that probe the boundaries of the system's behavior. And third, it lets us evaluate safely, because an accident in simulation costs nothing.

The challenge, and this is where a lot of the interesting research lives, is realism. A simulator is only useful if the behavior you see in it predicts what will happen on the road. That breaks down in a couple of ways. One is sensor realism: do the camera and lidar signals you synthesize actually look like what the real sensors produce? The other, which I'd argue is harder, is behavioral realism. The other agents in the scene, the cars, the pedestrians, the cyclists, need to react to our vehicle the way real people would. If you just replay a logged scene and our vehicle behaves differently than it did in the log, the other agents don't respond, and the scenario becomes meaningless. So you need agents that are reactive and realistic, and increasingly we're building those with learned models trained on our real-world driving data rather than hand-written rules.

I'd also say simulation isn't a replacement for real-world testing. The two are complementary. Real-world driving is where you discover the things you didn't know to simulate, and simulation is where you make sure you've thoroughly covered the things you do know about. The loop between them, finding something on the road, bringing it into simulation, expanding it, validating the fix, and then confirming it in the real world again, is really how the whole system improves.

r001.rationale: It says simulation lets teams test rare, unusual events such as pedestrians stepping out or cyclists running red lights, which are too uncommon or dangerous to test routinely on public roads.

r002.rationale: It describes building reactive simulator agents with learned models trained on real-world driving data, communicating the use of machine learning in simulator construction.

astra-6.text:
Simulators are a very important part of testing self-driving vehicles because they let you explore situations that are difficult to encounter repeatedly in the real world. If you see an interesting interaction on the road, you can recreate it in simulation and vary it: What if the pedestrian stepped out a little earlier? What if another vehicle was moving faster? That gives you a way to probe how robust the system is, rather than just asking whether it handled one particular example.

The challenge is making sure the simulation is meaningful. Other road users react to what your vehicle does, so you need to capture that interaction. And depending on what you’re testing, you may also need realistic sensor inputs. A simulator can give you very precise measurements, but those measurements are only useful if the simulated world captures the things that matter.

So I see simulation as complementary to real-world testing. You use real-world experience to improve and validate the simulator, and then use simulation to test more broadly and catch regressions as you change the system. It’s a powerful tool, but it isn’t, by itself, proof that a vehicle is safe.

r001.rationale: The response says simulation can recreate and vary difficult-to-encounter road interactions, including a pedestrian stepping out earlier, to test system robustness.

r002.rationale: It discusses simulation generally but does not propose using machine learning to build simulators.

sol-6.1.text:
I think simulation is a very important part of the testing process, because you can’t get all the coverage you need just by driving on public roads. Some of the situations we care most about are rare, and you want to be able to test them repeatedly without putting anyone at risk.

For example, you can take a challenging interaction from real-world driving and replay it in simulation, then vary things like the timing, the speed of the vehicles, or what a pedestrian does. That lets you explore how robust the system is, and also check that a software change hasn’t introduced a regression.

The challenge is making sure the simulator is representative of the real world. Other road users need to behave plausibly, and the aspects of the environment that matter to the system need to be modeled accurately. So I see simulation and real-world testing as complementary. Real-world data helps you improve and validate the simulator, and simulation lets you test at a scale and with a degree of control that driving alone can’t provide.

r001.rationale: It describes testing rare situations by varying what a pedestrian or other road user does in simulation.

r002.rationale: It discusses using simulation for testing but does not propose using machine learning to build the simulator.
